films.text: Quick lane, this one’s easy — and it starts with a question your customer has never been asked in their life. Watch what happens. They’ll pause. Because they don’t know what that means, and they can’t tell you no without finding out first. That’s the whole opening. You didn’t tell them anything was wrong. You didn’t ask if their air was cold enough. You asked whether they’d done something better — and now they want to know what it is. “No? Well — what we do is install a product directly into your A/C system that makes your air blow colder and get colder faster. It’s a one-time deal. As long as your system doesn’t leak, it lasts.” “Maximized” isn’t a repair word. Nothing is broken. Nothing is dirty. Nothing is worn out. You’re not fixing their car — you’re improving it. That’s a completely different conversation than everything else you sell all day, and customers hear the difference immediately. “Colder and colder faster.” Two benefits, both of which the customer will actually notice, both of which they care about in July. Not a maintenance interval. Not a prevented failure someday. Colder air, sooner. “One-time deal.” This is the strongest thing in the sentence. Everything else on your drive is recurring — you’ll be back for this, and back again. This one you do once. That’s rare, and customers like buying something that doesn’t come around again. “As long as it doesn’t leak.” Honest, and it costs you nothing. You just told them the one condition under which it wouldn’t hold. That small honesty is worth more than the sentence takes. It goes in while the 5,000-mile service is happening. No additional time. “It’s [$XX], and it happens while we’re already doing your 5,000-mile service, so you’re not here any minute longer. All I need is your approval.” …and that’s your 4-Step Close. What they need, what it costs, no extra time, and the ask — as a statement. Never end a presentation with a question. Don’t say their A/C is weak. You haven’t measured anything, and a customer whose air is fine will tell you so. Maximized works precisely because it doesn’t require anything to be wrong. Don’t promise a number. No degrees, no percentages, no “it’ll be twenty degrees colder.” Colder and faster. That’s what you say. Don’t sell it on smell. Different service, same rule as always. That’s the evaporator conversation, and it’s not this one. Don’t call it a recharge. It isn’t. If their system is genuinely low, that’s a diagnosis and a specialist, and this doesn’t substitute for it. Selling a maximizer to somebody with a real leak means they’re back in three weeks unhappy. First hot week of the year is when this sells itself. Everybody just turned their A/C on for the first time in six months. Ask the question every single car, all spring. Some of them will say yes before you finish. Do open with the question. Let them ask what it means. Do say “one-time deal.” It’s your best line. Don’t suggest anything’s wrong with their system. Let it go. Hector’s about to look at the whole vehicle, and the A/C conversation gets easier once there’s a report card on the desk.

The drive is where you ask the question. The kiosk is where you show them the whole picture. Because here’s the thing about Arctic Blast — it’s good on its own, but it’s part of something bigger, and this is the desk where that becomes obvious. Cabin air filter. Fresh filter, better airflow, and it’s the front door to everything else. A/C evaporator cleaning. Your filter catches what it can, but the fine stuff gets past it and settles on the evaporator — the cold, damp part of the system. Every A/C system does this. We run a treatment through and clear it out. Arctic Blast. The product that goes directly into the system to make the air blow colder and get colder faster. One-time deal. Look at what those three do together. You clean what’s coming in, you clean what it lands on, and then you maximize what comes out. Air in, air through, air out. That’s not three upsells stapled together. That’s one system, start to finish — and the customer can follow it, because it’s the same air the whole way. “Mr. Smith, thanks for coming in. While we’ve got your Camry, I want to show you something we call Beat the Heat.” “There are three things that make your air conditioning work. The filter that pulls air in, the evaporator that cools it, and the system that pushes it out. We take care of all three. New cabin air filter. A treatment through the evaporator to clear it out — every A/C system needs that one. And a product that goes right into the system to make your air blow colder and get colder faster.” “All three together is [$XXX], which saves you [20%] over doing them separately. And it all happens while we’re already doing your 5,000-mile service, so you’re not here any minute longer. All I need is your approval.” What does the customer need? — all three, one system Authorization. — all I need is your approval Offer three separate services and the customer says yes to one and no to two. That’s how it goes. They’re doing math on each item as it lands, and by the third one they’re just declining on principle. Offer one thing and they make one decision. The bundle also protects you from something the odor script warned about — one off-menu item per presentation. Three separate pitches violates that. One bundle doesn’t, because it’s one thing with three parts. And the savings are real. Say the number. Lead with the filter. It’s the one they’ve heard of, it’s the one Hector’s going to photograph, and it’s the easiest thing to picture. Then the evaporator, because the filter makes it make sense — the filter catches what it can, but some gets past. Then Arctic Blast last, because it’s the only one that’s an improvement rather than a maintenance item. Ending on “colder and faster” leaves them with the good part. Never sell on smell. Even inside the bundle. Every A/C system does this — that’s the frame, and it doesn’t change because there are three services now. Don’t promise a temperature. Colder and faster. That’s what you say. Don’t sell Beat the Heat to cover a real problem. If the customer’s air genuinely isn’t cold, that’s a diagnosis, a specialist, and a different op code. This bundle makes a working system work better. It doesn’t fix a broken one, and selling it that way means they’re back in three weeks unhappy with all three. “Absolutely. Let’s do the filter today, and we’ll look at the rest next time.” Then note it. That’s next visit’s pre-write packet, and Beat the Heat is a better conversation the second time when they already know what it is.

Quick lane setup, and this op code has a wrinkle worth naming. There’s nothing on the multi-point that says “needs Arctic Blast.” Hector grades 27 items. None of them is “this A/C could be more maximized.” There’s no reading, no measurement, no yellow or red that points at this service. That’s because nothing is wrong. This is an improvement, not a repair, and improvements don’t show up on inspection sheets. The cabin filter. That’s your door back in. Hector’s going to pull that filter and photograph it. If it’s dirty, you’ve got a picture — and that picture is the front end of the same system Arctic Blast lives at the back of. Air in, air through, air out. The filter photo gets you into the first part of that sentence, and the rest follows naturally. “Mr. Smith, while you’re relaxing in our lounge — my certified technician Hector is doing a full multi-point inspection on your Camry along with your 5,000-mile service. He grades everything green, yellow, or red. Your battery cranking amps, your tire tread depth, the condition of your filters. When he’s finished I’ll come find you and we’ll go through the results together. Should be about twenty minutes.” “The condition of your filters.” That’s the slot, and on this op code it’s the whole play. Say filters and you’ve teed up the cabin filter, which tees up the evaporator, which tees up Arctic Blast. Never say “oil change.” We don’t do oil changes. We do 5,000-mile services, 7,500-mile services, 10,000-mile services. An oil change is a commodity somebody buys on price. A 5,000-mile service is a scheduled maintenance event that happens to include oil. Never say the customer is “waiting.” Waiting is what you do at the DMV. They’re relaxing in your lounge. Enjoying a cup of coffee. Take a load off. Same twenty minutes, completely different twenty minutes. And here’s why the inspection matters at all Somebody can get their oil changed at Walmart. At a quick lube down the street. In a parking lot from a van. So what’s the actual difference between here and there? They can get oil anywhere. They cannot get a certified technician putting eyes on twenty-seven items and grading every one, with photos, handed to somebody who’ll walk them through it. That’s not an upsell. That’s the reason to pull in here instead of there — and most of your customers have never had anybody explain it to them. Don’t mention it here. Don’t say “we’ll revisit that A/C package.” You’re setting up the inspection, not relitigating a decision they already made twenty minutes ago. Let the filter photo reopen it on its own. If they already said yes to Beat the Heat — say so, right here. “And Hector’s going to take care of that Beat the Heat package while he’s in there, so that’ll be done when you leave today.” Small thing. But a customer who just spent money likes hearing that it’s already happening. That’s the difference between a purchase and a promise. For the details and the depth, go to our “Get The Hell Outta Here” section and get certified in that speech.

Hector’s done, and everything came back green. A lot of advisors let this one go. No red, no yellow, nothing to sell — so they hand over the keys, say the car looks great, and move on to the next one. That’s a mistake, and here’s why. The all-green customer is your best customer. They take care of their vehicle. They come back. They approve things when there’s a reason. And you’re about to send them home without telling them a single thing they did right. Go get them — and bring them to your kiosk. “Mr. Smith — I’ve got your Camry’s inspection back. Come on over to my desk and I’ll walk you through it.” Never sell in the lounge. That’s their business, not the room’s. And the next customer is sitting right there — if they’ve already heard your whole presentation, it doesn’t land when you use it on them in twenty minutes. “Mr. Smith, first, thank you for bringing your Camry to us. This is the 7th visit you’ve made to our humble establishment. That means something to us.” “Hector graded your Camry on 27 items — green, yellow, and red. And I want you to hear this: everything came back green. All 27. Your battery cranking amps, your tire tread depth, your fluids, your filters. Every one.” “That doesn’t happen by accident. That’s you staying on top of this thing, and it’s the reason this Camry’s going to go another hundred thousand miles.” This is REWARD ACTION, and it’s the whole point of the principle. Most customers only ever hear from us when something’s wrong. This one just heard that everything’s right, and that they’re the reason. That is a customer who comes back. That is a customer who tells somebody. And it cost you thirty seconds. Then — and only then — the one thing left. “So there’s nothing your Camry needs today. But there is one thing it could use.” “Remember when I asked if you’d had your A/C maximized? Everything in your system is healthy — Hector confirmed it. That’s actually the best time to do this, because we’re not fixing anything, we’re just making a good system better. The product goes right in, your air blows colder and gets colder faster, and it’s a one-time deal. As long as it doesn’t leak, it lasts.” “It’s [$XX], Hector can do it right now while he’s finishing up, so you’re not here any minute longer. All I need is your approval.” Why the re-pitch works better here than it did on the drive. On the drive you asked a stranger a question. Now you’ve got proof. “Everything is healthy — that’s why this is the right time.” You just turned all-green from a reason to say no into the reason to say yes. A maximizer belongs on a system in good shape. You have documentation that theirs is. Nothing else is competing for the money. There’s no red item, no yellow, no four-hundred-dollar decision in front of them. This is the only ask on the desk, and it’s a small one. You just told them they’ve been doing it right. People who’ve been praised say yes more than people who’ve been corrected. That’s not a trick — it’s just what happens when somebody feels good about their car. Notice the ask is a statement. All I need is your approval. Never end a presentation with a question. Fine. You still did the most important thing today. “No problem at all. Your Camry’s in great shape and you should be proud of that. I’ll note it and we’ll talk about it next time.” That customer leaves feeling good, with a car that’s green across the board, and a note in the system for next visit. Even on an all-green car — if the cabin filter is anywhere close to due, Beat the Heat is still the better ask than Arctic Blast alone.

Step five of your walk-around. Hit the windshield washer fluid. Most advisors treat that step as a fluid-level check. It isn’t. That’s the wiper sale, and it happens in three seconds on every single car that pulls in. You just made those blades run across wet glass with the customer sitting right there watching. Whatever they do, they do it in front of both of you. Streaking. A line of water left behind on every pass. Chattering. That skip and shudder across the glass. Missed spots. A section the blade doesn’t touch at all. Hazing. The windshield goes cloudy instead of clear. Any one of those and you don’t have to say a word about condition. They saw it. Say what they’re doing, not what they are Not “your wipers are bad.” Not “those are shot.” Not “man, those are old.” Streaking is a condition. It’s what the blade is doing, right now, on their glass, and they just watched it happen. That’s not an opinion they can argue with — it’s a fact you both observed. Same thing Hector does on the multi-point. He doesn’t say a part looks worn out. He says what it’s doing. “See how that’s streaking? That’s the rubber edge giving out. We can put a new set on for [$XX], and we’ll have it done while we’re doing your 5,000-mile service. All I need is your approval.” …and that’s your 4-Step Close. What they need, what it costs, when it’s done, and the ask as a statement. Never end a presentation with a question. This is the sale almost nobody makes, and it’s sitting on half the vehicles on your drive. Every SUV, every wagon, every hatchback, every minivan has one. And here’s the thing: the rear blade is usually in worse shape than the fronts, for two reasons. It gets used a fraction as often, so the rubber sits and hardens instead of staying flexible. And it lives on the back of the vehicle taking direct sun all day with nothing shading it. The customer has no idea. They see the front ones working every time it rains. They see the back one maybe twice a year when they’re backing out in a storm. “And you’ve got a rear blade back there too — most folks forget it’s there. Let me have Hector check that one while he’s got the new set out.” Walk to the back and run it if you can. Same trick as the front — let them watch it. One conversation, two sales. You’re already selling wipers. Adding the rear blade costs you eight seconds and it’s the single most commonly missed piggyback in the shop. Don’t drop to a cheaper option first. Tell them why the number is the number. “I hear you. We only want to put the best wipers on your beautiful Camry. Those are the ones built for your vehicle, and they’re the ones that’ll still be clearing your glass next winter.” “Your beautiful Camry.” Say it. That’s a car this person picked out, paid for, and drives every day. Two words and you’ve told them you see it the way they do. And notice what that answer does. It doesn’t apologize for the price and it doesn’t argue about it. It just says: this is what good costs, and your car is worth good. Some of them will say yes right there. That’s the whole reason you don’t lead with the cheap option — you never find out they’d have paid for the good one. “If you’d rather, we can do the refills instead of the whole blade. That replaces the rubber, which is the part that actually wore out.” That’s your value option and it’s a real one. But it comes second, after they’ve heard the case for the best ones. Lead with inserts and you’ve made the decision for them. Do hit the washer fluid on every car. Every one. It costs three seconds. Do say streaking, chattering, missed spots. Conditions, not opinions. Do check the back of every SUV, wagon, hatchback, and minivan. Don’t say their wipers are bad, shot, or nasty. That’s a judgment. Don’t skip the rear blade because you’re busy. It’s eight seconds. Don’t lead with inserts. That’s your answer to price, not your opening. Let it go. Hector’s grading the wipers on the multi-point anyway, and this is one of the easiest items on that sheet to document — a photo of a torn or cracked blade needs no explanation at all. You’ll have another shot with evidence in your hand.

Whether you hit the washer fluid or not, there is still ample opportunity to offer someone a set of wipers. And this one has a different voice behind it. On the drive, the vehicle was doing the talking — those blades streaked in front of both of you. Here, at your kiosk, it’s you and your store. Based on time, mileage, and the condition of the Camry. Wipers are one of the few things on your menu where time beats mileage every time. A car that sits in a driveway all year has the same six-month-old rubber as one that drove thirty thousand miles. Sun, heat, and cold are what kill a blade, not use. Most manufacturers land somewhere around six months to a year. And condition here is mostly about where the car lives — hot sun, hard winters, or parked outside instead of in a garage. “Mr. Smith, thank you so much for entrusting us with your Camry. After completing a review of your history, at this stage in your Camry’s life there are a few key maintenance services we highly recommend to keep it running smoothly and reliably for years to come. We’ve bundled these to maximize savings and safety. My favorite part of the [30,000]-mile service package is the wiper blades. Are you familiar with our wiper blades?” “What we’re doing is getting rid of your old wiper blades that have done their job, and putting on a brand-new Toyota set. Those are built for your Camry and they’ll still be clearing your glass next winter. This package would be a total investment of [$XXX], and we can have it done by [2:30]. All I need is your approval.” What does the customer need? — new blades Authorization. — all I need is your approval Say the brand. Same reason as the filter. Two words and the part stops being a generic blade off a shelf and starts being the one built for this vehicle. Half the vehicles at your desk have one. It’s usually in worse shape than the fronts — it sits unused so the rubber hardens, and it takes direct sun all day with nothing shading it. “And your Camry’s got a rear blade as well. Most folks forget it’s there. Let me have Hector take care of that one too while he’s at it.” This is the one that makes the wiper conversation bigger than wipers. “One more thing. While we’ve got the glass in front of us — we do a windshield treatment. It bonds right to the glass and makes it hydrophobic, so rain beads up and rolls off instead of sitting there. Your wipers work less. Ice and snow clear easier. It cuts the glare from oncoming headlights at night. Bugs and bird droppings wipe right off.” Look at what that does with the wipers. New blades clear the glass. The treatment means there’s less to clear. Sold together, they’re not two items — they’re one outcome, which is you can see. That’s the frame. Everything on this desk is about vision. For the details on that service — how it goes on, how long it takes, what the customer needs to know afterward — go to the product knowledge series. Know that material before you offer it. If you’re doing the whole vision package — front blades, rear blade, windshield treatment — that’s one bundle, one price, one decision. Don’t pitch it as three separate items. Offer three things and a customer says yes to one and no to two. “All three together is [$XXX], which saves you [20%] over doing them separately.” “I hear you. We only want to put the best wipers on your beautiful Camry.” Then, if they still need it, inserts. That replaces the rubber, which is the part that actually wore out. Real value option — it just comes second. “No problem at all, Mr. Smith. Let me have our certified technician Hector take a look, and we’ll go over how he grades your Camry.” And on wipers that’s a strong position. A photo of a cracked or torn blade needs no explanation at all.

Say you didn’t do pre-writes. You never hit the washer fluid. No menus, no kiosk time. You’ve still got the best shot of the day coming. The VERY BEST way to sell a set of wipers — or anything else — is after a great multi-point inspection by your certified technicians. So after your write-up, just before the customer takes off or heads to your lounge, give this speech. “Mr. Smith, before you take off to go shopping, I wanted to share with you what’s next. My certified technician Hector is going to be completing your [5,000-mile] service today. While he’s doing that, he does a really thorough multi-point inspection, including a 90-second highlight video. You’ll get to see some parts of your Camry you don’t normally see. He grades things on a GYR scale — like your battery cranking amps, your tire tread depth, and the condition of your wiper blades. If there are any items in yellow or red, we’re going to text you his recommendations. The quickest way to get your Camry back is to select the green ‘approve’ button. And if I don’t hear back from you, do you mind if I give you a quick call?” On coolant it was the condition of your coolant. On the differential, the condition of your gear oil. Here it’s the condition of your wiper blades. Same speech. One swap. And you just planted the exact thing you’re going to sell in twenty minutes. That’s the whole trick with this stage. Whatever you’re going after today goes in that third slot. And on this op code, that swap does something extra. Wipers are the one item on the inspection sheet the customer can verify themselves. They can’t check their own cranking amps. They can’t measure tread depth or read gear oil. But the second you say “wiper blades” out loud, they’re going to think about the last time it rained — and a lot of them already know the answer. You just handed them a question they can answer on their own while they’re gone. Half of them will have decided before your text ever arrives. A torn blade. A cracked edge. Rubber separating from the frame. That picture needs no explanation, no analogy, no dollar comparison. It looks exactly as bad as it is. For the details and the depth, go to our “Get The Hell Outta Here” section and get certified in that speech. A speech like that sets your certified technician up perfectly.

OK. You didn’t do pre-writes. You never hit the washer fluid. No menus, no kiosk time. But you set up the multi-point well — and now we’re going to capitalize. When you’re speaking to a customer, focus on what CAN be done instead of what CANNOT be done. Be positive. Be upbeat. Use positive language. REWARD ACTION. When a customer has done the right thing, tell them. And you gotta really SING this one. If you’re bored, the customer will be too. “Mr. Smith, our certified technician Hector has completed the multi-point inspection that you requested, and I got the notification that you received your video. If you have a minute, I’d like to go over some of the details.” “First, I want to thank you for bringing your Camry to me. I’m not sure if you’re aware, but this is the 7th visit you and your Camry have made to our humble establishment. Thank you for being a loyal customer.” “Your Camry has [30,000] miles, and as you saw, Hector graded your vehicle on 27 items using that green, yellow, and red standard.” “He measured your battery cranking amps — those came back green. He checked your tire tread depth — green as well. We want to keep a good eye on both of those.” “However, based on time, mileage, and the condition of your wiper blades, Hector recommends replacing them.” “Are you familiar with our wiper blades?” If yes: “Great — then you know how important it is.” Straight to the close. “What we’re doing is getting rid of your old wiper blades that have done their job, and putting on a brand-new Toyota set. Those are built for your Camry, and they’ll still be clearing your glass next winter.” “Take a look at Hector’s photo. See that edge? That’s the rubber separating from the frame. That’s what streaking looks like before you see it on the glass.” “And your Camry’s got a rear blade as well — most folks forget it’s back there. It’s usually in worse shape than the fronts, because it sits unused and it takes full sun all day.” “Those items, along with your oil change, tire rotation, and the other items on your service, bring your total investment to [$XXX.XX], and we can have it completed by [3:00]. All I need is your approval.” First — the photo does the work. A torn blade or a cracked edge needs no explanation, no analogy, no dollar comparison. Hand them the picture and be quiet for a second. This is one of the easiest closes on the whole inspection sheet. Second, and this is the one I want you to remember: I don’t care why that customer came in today. Oil change. Brake noise. Check engine light. Recall. State inspection. Somebody else’s mistake. If those blades are streaking, that conversation happens. Every time. Every visit. Every customer. Here’s why. Wipers are the only thing on that vehicle standing between your customer and not being able to see. Everything else you sell them protects a part. This one protects them. And it’s the cheapest item on your menu. There’s no reason for anybody to drive out of your shop unable to see in the rain because their advisor was too busy to mention it. So don’t skip it because the ticket’s already big. Don’t skip it because they came in for something else. Don’t skip it because it’s only forty dollars and you’ve got three other cars. Everybody deserves wipers. Every visit, every time.

Step three of your walk-around. Start the car — listen and look. A serpentine belt that’s slipping tells on itself the second that engine turns over. Squeal. Chirp. A screech on a cold start that fades after a few seconds. If you’re standing there and it happens, you both heard it. But here’s the part I really need you to hear. You cannot eyeball a modern serpentine belt. Old belts cracked. They frayed. They glazed up so you could see it. Those days are gone — modern belts are made from a material that wears down instead of cracking apart, and the overwhelming majority of belt failures happen on belts that look completely fine. No cracks. No fraying. Nothing an advisor or a customer would ever spot. So if you pop the hood, look at that belt, and tell a customer it looks good — you may have just told them something that isn’t true. And if it strands them next month, that’s the conversation you’re going to remember. What actually finds it is a measurement. There’s a gauge that reads the depth of the ribs on the belt. That’s the real wear, and Hector has one. Which means on this op code your job is not to assess. It’s to get it measured. “Did you catch that squeal on startup? That’s your serpentine belt slipping. I want to have Hector put a gauge on it — modern belts wear down instead of cracking, so you can’t tell by looking. He can measure it and we’ll know for sure.” Most cars don’t squeal. That doesn’t mean the belt’s fine — it means it hasn’t started slipping yet. Use the mileage instead. Most manufacturers want that belt inspected around 30,000 miles and replaced somewhere between 60,000 and 100,000. Know your brand’s numbers. “You’re at [65,000] — that’s right in the window where these get replaced. Let me have Hector measure it while he’s in there. Costs you nothing to know.” Customers think a belt is a rubber loop. Tell them what it actually does. “That one belt runs your alternator, your water pump, and your power steering. If it lets go, you don’t coast to a shop — you lose your charging, your steering gets heavy, and your engine starts overheating, all at the same time. It’s a small part that everything else depends on.” That’s not a scare tactic. That’s just what happens, and it’s the difference between a customer hearing “belt” and a customer hearing “the thing that keeps everything else running.” The piggyback — and this one is not optional Put a new belt on a worn tensioner and it squeals again in a few weeks. Customer comes back angry, you look bad, and now you’re doing it twice for free. “And when Hector measures the belt, he’ll check the tensioner too. Those two work as a pair — putting a new belt on a tired tensioner is how you end up right back here.” Say that up front, before the work, not after. A customer who hears it in advance understands why the ticket is what it is. A customer who hears it after a comeback thinks you missed something. One more thing — if it’s an EV, skip it entirely Electric vehicles don’t have serpentine belts. The motors drive the accessories directly. Pitch a belt inspection on an EV and that customer will look it up. Same rule as power steering fluid on an electric rack, same rule as a rear differential on a front-wheel-drive car. Know what’s in front of you before you open your mouth. Do listen on startup. Every car. It’s already step three. Do get it measured. That’s the whole job on this op code. Do price the tensioner with it, up front. Don’t tell a customer the belt looks good. You can’t know that. Don’t confuse it with a timing belt. Different part, different service, wildly different consequence. Let it go. Hector’s going to measure it anyway and put a number on the sheet — and a number beats anything you or I could say out here.

Whether you heard a squeal or not — whether you popped the hood or not — there is still ample opportunity to offer someone a belt inspection. And this one has a different voice behind it. On the drive, the vehicle was doing the talking. Here, at your kiosk, it’s you and your store. But this op code has a limit, and I want you to respect it. You cannot sell a belt from behind a desk. You don’t know its condition. Neither does the customer. Modern belts wear down instead of cracking, so the overwhelming majority of failures happen on belts that look completely fine — and looking is all anybody’s done so far. So at the kiosk, you are not selling a belt. You’re selling the measurement. Based on time, mileage, and the condition of the Camry. Most manufacturers want the belt inspected around 30,000 miles, with replacement typically landing between 60,000 and 100,000. Know your brand’s numbers cold. That inspection interval is your opening, and it’s a factory recommendation, not your opinion. “You’re at [65,000], and your manufacturer wants that belt inspected every 30,000. Let me have Hector measure it while he’s in there.” “Mr. Smith, thank you so much for entrusting us with your Camry. Whatever comes back green today, that one’s still on the calendar.” Say it. Every time. Even if they already told you no on the belt. Because the worst version of this op code isn’t losing the sale. It’s a customer who declines the belt in the morning, gets an all-green inspection in the afternoon, and drives away thinking that settled it. “Mr. Smith, before you take off to go shopping, I wanted to share with you what’s next. My certified technician Hector is going to be completing your [5,000-mile] service today. While he’s doing that, he does a really thorough multi-point inspection, including a 90-second highlight video. You’ll get to see some parts of your Camry you don’t normally see. He grades things on a GYR scale — like your battery cranking amps, your tire tread depth, and the condition of your fluids and filters. If there are any items in yellow or red, we’re going to text you his recommendations. The quickest way to get your Camry back is to select the green ‘approve’ button. And if I don’t hear back from you, do you mind if I give you a quick call?” Notice the third item is generic here — fluids and filters. That’s on purpose. There’s nothing timing-belt-specific to put in that slot, so you use the default and let the inspection be the inspection. He can’t see the belt, but he can see what’s around it. Coolant or oil seeping near the front of the engine, staining around the timing cover, a weep from the water pump area — those show up on an inspection, and they point straight at this job. If that comes back, you’ve got something the drive conversation didn’t have. Not proof about the belt, but a real reason the front of that engine needs to come apart soon anyway. And if it’s coming apart anyway, the belt goes with it. For the details and the depth, go to our “Get The Hell Outta Here” section and get certified in that speech.

OK. Hector’s done, and now you’ve got a decision to make that no other op code puts in front of you. Because there are two versions of this conversation, and which one you’re having depends on something that has nothing to do with the timing belt. When you’re speaking to a customer, focus on what CAN be done instead of what CANNOT be done. Be positive. Be upbeat. Use positive language. REWARD ACTION. When a customer has done the right thing, tell them. “Mr. Smith, our certified technician Hector has completed the multi-point inspection that you requested, and I got the notification that you received your video. If you have a minute, I’d like to go over some of the details.” “First, I want to thank you for bringing your Camry to me. I’m not sure if you’re aware, but this is the 7th visit you and your Camry have made to our humble establishment. Thank you for being a loyal customer.” “Your Camry has [95,000] miles, and as you saw, Hector graded your vehicle on 27 items using that green, yellow, and red standard.” “He measured your battery cranking amps — those came back green. He checked your tire tread depth — green as well. We want to keep a good eye on both of those.” VERSION ONE — Hector saw something at the front of the engine This is the one you want. He couldn’t see the belt, but he could see around it — a seep at the timing cover, staining, a weep from the water pump area. “However, Hector did note some seepage at the front of your engine, right around the timing cover.” “Here’s why that matters, and it ties right back to what we talked about this morning. To fix that seep, the front of your engine has to come apart. And once it’s apart, your timing belt is sitting right there.” “You’re at [95,000] and that belt is due at [100,000]. So this is the visit where doing both together costs a fraction of doing them separately — because the expensive part of a timing belt job isn’t the belt. It’s getting to it.” “What we’re doing is replacing that belt along with the water pump and the pulleys, all at the same time, while everything’s already open. That’s going to help with the performance of your Camry and help you avoid the kind of failure that ends an engine.” “Those items, along with your oil change, tire rotation, and the other items on your service, bring your total investment to [$X,XXX.XX], and we can have it completed by [3:00]. All I need is your approval.” Why this version closes. You didn’t find the belt. You found a reason the engine is coming apart anyway — and the belt is the cheapest thing you’ll ever add to a job that’s already happening. You’ve got an all-green inspection and a customer who’s about to feel great about their car. “And I’ve got good news — everything else came back green. All 27 items. That doesn’t happen by accident. That’s you staying on top of this thing.” Then close the gap. This is the part you cannot skip. “Now, one thing I want to be straight with you about. That timing belt we talked about this morning isn’t on this report. Hector would have to take the front of your engine apart to look at it, so it’s not something he can grade.” “So this green report means everything he could check is in good shape. It doesn’t mean the belt is. That one’s still a calendar item, and you’re at [95,000] with a [100,000] interval.” “I’d rather tell you that than let a clean report do the talking for something it doesn’t cover.” Then either close it or defer it properly. “This service runs [$X,XXX] and includes the water pump and pulleys, because they come out with the belt. We can have it done by [3:00]. All I need is your approval.” “No problem at all. I’m going to note it as deferred — not declined — at [95,000] miles, so it’s right at the top of your file next time you’re in.” First — the all-green report is the danger. A customer with a clean inspection and an overdue belt is worse off than one who never got inspected, because now they’ve got a document telling them everything’s fine. Closing that gap out loud is the most important thing you do on this op code, and it’s worth more than the sale. Second — the labor argument is the entire close. The belt is cheap. Getting to it is not. Every version of this conversation comes back to: it’s already apart, or it’s going to have to come apart, so do it once. Third — this one grades red on any visit, except it doesn’t grade at all. Unlike a hose or a belt or a battery, nothing puts this on the sheet. It only ever surfaces because somebody looked at the mileage. That somebody is you. If you don’t bring it up, nobody in the building will. And don’t forget your piggyback sales. Water pump and pulleys, every time, priced in from the start.
